name: Dimmer Switch
tagline: It chops the mains waveform instead of just switching it — which is why the lamp has to match the dimmer.
terminals: Load — dimmed live out to the lamps
Earth — functional earth or plate earth as the design requires
parts: Rotary knob or slider — the control you turn
Rear module — the electronics and the heat sink behind the plate
safety: Match the dimmer to the load. Leading-edge dimmers suit most incandescent and halogen lamps; trailing-edge suits electronic transformers and most LED lamps. A mismatched dimmer buzzes, flickers, will not dim to zero, and can destroy an LED driver. Total load must sit between the dimmer’s minimum and maximum.

points.label: Faceplate
points.detail: A dimmer plate looks like any other, but the unit behind it is deeper and gets warm. Plate and back box both need the depth, and the load rating has to cover the total wattage of every lamp on the circuit.

points.label: Rotary knob
points.detail: Turn to set the level; push to switch on many designs. The knob drives either a potentiometer on older leading-edge units or an encoder on electronic ones — in both cases it is setting the point in each half cycle at which the device switches the load on.

points.label: Fixing screws
points.detail: Two screws into the back box. If the plate sits proud, do not pull it down with the screws: the heat sink needs air behind the plate and a distorted plate can jam the knob.

points.label: Rear module and heat sink
points.detail: The electronics live in the moulding behind the plate and dump their heat through the finned metal body. Dimmers are rated with that heat sink in free air — burying the plate behind curtains or insulating it in a sealed back box derates it and shortens its life.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a dimmer switch showing the TRIAC on its heat sink, suppression choke, potentiometer and timing network

cutawayPoints.label: TRIAC
cutawayPoints.detail: The semiconductor that does the dimming: it turns on partway through each half cycle and switches off at the zero crossing. It is bolted to metal because while it conducts it still drops a volt or two, and at full load that is several watts of heat in a plastic box.

cutawayPoints.label: Heat sink
cutawayPoints.detail: The finned aluminium the TRIAC is mounted on, and the reason a dimmer is derated when it is stacked alongside others in a multi-gang plate: less heat sink per dimmer, so less load each may carry. It is also why a dimmer in a sealed or insulated box runs hotter than one in free air.

cutawayPoints.label: Suppression choke
cutawayPoints.detail: A coil in series with the load that slows the sharp switching edge of the TRIAC. Without it the edge makes the lamp filament or the driver buzz audibly and sprays radio-frequency interference back down the wiring — the hum you can hear through a radio in the same room.

cutawayPoints.label: Setting potentiometer
cutawayPoints.detail: The track behind the knob, setting how far into each half cycle the TRIAC fires. On LED-friendly designs there is also a minimum-load trim, because a lamp that draws a few watts may never pull enough current to keep an old dimmer timing circuit stable.

cutawayPoints.label: DIAC and RC network
cutawayPoints.detail: A capacitor charges through a resistor each half cycle and the DIAC fires the TRIAC when it reaches its threshold. Moving that firing point earlier or later is all a dimmer does — it never reduces the voltage, it just conducts for a shorter slice of each half cycle.

cutawayPoints.label: Rear terminals
cutawayPoints.detail: Two terminals, wired in series with the live exactly like a switch, and no neutral — which is why a smart dimmer that needs one may not fit an existing back box, and why a dimmer cannot simply be dropped into a two-way arrangement without the right companion switch.
